item.title: Why do we find it hard to resist the temptation of "free"?
item.description: An analysis from the perspective of microeconomics and psychology: Why 'free' leads people to impulsive consumption, even when those things are unnecessary.
item.content:encoded:
When we frantically grab things we don’t need, especially under the temptation of “free,” it may seem irrational, but deep explanations can be found from the perspectives of microeconomics and psychology.

Analysis from the Perspective of Microeconomics:

  1. “Zero Price Effect”: This is a very important concept in behavioral economics, specifically used to explain the magic of “free.” Traditional economics suggests that price is merely a quantitative indicator; a price decrease increases demand, but a drop to zero is just a linear extension of increased demand. However, behavioral economics points out that “free” is not just a price of zero; it represents a qualitative leap psychologically, completely changing people’s decision-making patterns.

    • Reducing Transaction Costs and Psychological Friction: Buying anything requires paying a cost, not just in money, but also in decision-making costs, time costs, and even the psychological “pain of paying.” “Free” completely eliminates these costs and friction. People don’t need to weigh pros and cons or consider if it’s worth it; they just “take” it, greatly reducing the difficulty and psychological threshold of the decision.
    • Risk Aversion and Preference for Certainty: Even for a very small item, if it is “free,” it means “zero risk.” In contrast, buying anything that requires money carries potential risks, such as buying something you dislike or of poor quality. Free items guarantee “at least no loss,” and this certain gain is highly attractive to risk-averse individuals.
    • Value Perception Bias: When the price is zero, people’s perception of an item’s value becomes distorted. We tend to overestimate the value of free items, even if we don’t actually need them. This bias might be because “free” activates the regions in our brain associated with “gaining” and “reward,” making us feel like we got a bargain.

  2. Misjudgment of Opportunity Cost: Traditional economics emphasizes opportunity cost—the value of the highest opportunity forgone in order to obtain something. Rational people weigh the benefits of obtaining a free item against the opportunity cost incurred (such as the time spent queuing, the space occupied, etc.). However, under the temptation of “free,” we often underestimate or ignore the opportunity cost.

    • Neglect of Time Value: To claim a free item, we might need to queue, run errands, or spend extra time. But the halo of “free” often makes us feel that this time expenditure is worthwhile, even ignoring the fact that this time could have been used for something more valuable.
    • Space and Resource Occupation: Free items that are frantically grabbed, if unnecessary, might occupy space in the home or even become trash. But when claiming these free items, we often fail to fully consider these subsequent costs.

  3. “Bargain Hunting” Psychology and Transaction Utility: Richard Thaler’s theory of “Transaction Utility” suggests that when people purchase goods, they simultaneously experience two types of utility: Acquisition Utility (satisfaction derived from the actual value of the goods) and Transaction Utility (the feeling derived from the difference between the actual paid price and the psychological reference price).

    • Super High Transaction Utility from “Free”: When the price is zero, transaction utility reaches its maximum because the actual paid price is far below the psychological reference price (even if the psychological reference price is low). This massive transaction utility makes us feel like we “made a huge profit,” even if the actual value of the goods is low or even negative.
    • The “If You Don’t Take It, You Lose It” Mentality: “Free” reinforces the “if you don’t take it, you lose it” mentality. Even if we don’t need it, the thought that others are grabbing it, or that this opportunity might disappear, makes us more likely to act impulsively to claim it.

Analysis from the Perspective of Psychology:

  1. Loss Aversion: This is a very important concept in both behavioral economics and psychology. People feel the pain of a loss more intensely than the pleasure of an equivalent gain.

    • Fear of Missing Out on “Free”: “Free” is often packaged as a limited-time or limited-quantity offer, creating a sense of scarcity and urgency. This atmosphere triggers our loss aversion, making us fear missing out on this “free” opportunity, even if we don’t truly need the items.
    • Weakening of the “Sunk Cost” Effect: For items that require payment, we consider the costs already invested (sunk costs) and hope to maximize their utilization. But for items obtained for free, since no monetary cost was incurred, the sunk cost effect is weaker, making us more likely to claim them impulsively, even if they might eventually be idle or wasted.

  2. Social Proof and Conformity: People tend to imitate the behavior of those around them, especially when uncertain or lacking information.

    • “Herd Behavior” and Group Action: When we see many people frantically grabbing free items, we assume the item must have value, or at least “not be a loss.” This conformity increases the frantic grabbing behavior, forming a “herd effect.”
    • Fear of Exclusion: If everyone goes to claim the free items and we don’t act, we might feel excluded by the group, or that we missed out on some kind of “social opportunity.”

  3. Instant Gratification and Impulsivity: Humans are naturally inclined to pursue instant gratification, and “free” perfectly satisfies this psychological need.

    • Quick Acquisition of Happiness and Satisfaction: The process of claiming free items is simple and fast, immediately providing a sense of happiness and satisfaction from “getting a bargain.” This instant gratification reinforces our impulsive behavior.
    • Weakening of Inhibitory Control: Under the temptation of “free,” we are more likely to relax our guard, reducing our capacity for rational thought and self-control, thus making us more prone to impulsive decisions.

  4. Anchoring Effect: When people make decisions, they tend to rely excessively on the first piece of information they receive (the anchor), even if that information is irrelevant to the decision.

    • “Free” as a Value Anchor: “Free” can serve as a value anchor, making us more likely to accept seemingly “worthwhile” discounts in subsequent consumption decisions, even if those discounts are not truly worthwhile.
    • Contrast Effect and Value Amplification: The existence of free items might make us feel that other items requiring payment are “more expensive,” thereby amplifying the perceived value of the free items.

Summary:

Our frantic grabbing of things we fundamentally don’t need, especially under the temptation of “free,” is the result of the combined action of various factors in microeconomics and psychology. “Free” is not just a price of zero; it is a powerful psychological lure that utilizes our Zero Price Effect, Loss Aversion, Social Proof, Instant Gratification, Anchoring Effect, and other psychological mechanisms, leading us to make seemingly irrational decisions driven by impulse.

So, what’s next? We can launch a marketing campaign called “Free Temptation.”

item.title: Why do we like comparison?
item.description: The anchoring effect reveals how people are influenced by initial information when making decisions. They often only clarify their own choices in specific contexts, and merchants cleverly leverage this psychological phenomenon to guide consumption.
item.content:encoded:
Anchoring Effect

Most people only realize what they truly want when they are in a specific situation.

  • We want to buy a road bike, but don’t know which model, until we see a champion from the Tour de France advertising a certain model and can then clarify what we want to purchase;
  • We want to upgrade our speakers, but don’t know what kind, until we hear a set that sounds better than our current ones and become clear;
  • We don’t even know how to live, until relatives or friends suddenly make us realize that the life they are living is exactly what we aspire to.

Everything is relative; that is the key point.

For example, Sam, the TV salesman, plays the same kind of trick on us when grouping the TVs on display: 36-inch Panasonic for $690. 42-inch Toshiba for $850. 50-inch Philips for $1,480.

Which one would you choose? Sam knows very well that customers find it difficult to calculate the value of different TVs. (Who can accurately know that the Panasonic for $690 is a better deal than the Philips for $1,480?) Sam also knows that after giving the customer three choices, most people will choose the one priced at $850. This feeling is like an airplane landing between two runway lights. Can you guess which brand Sam placed in the middle? Not bad, it is the one he wants to sell the most!

One phenomenon is that a high price tag on a main course on a menu can increase a restaurant’s profit—even if no one orders it. Why? Because even though people generally won’t order the most expensive dish on the menu, they are likely to order the second most expensive one. For this purpose, the restaurant introduces a high-priced dish, which tempts customers to order the next most expensive dish (thereby cleverly increasing the profit margin on that dish).

item.title: How to Activate Your Critical Thinking Radar: A Practical Guide to Identifying Information Manipulation
item.description: This article details how to effectively identify potential manipulative techniques within information through structured questioning and multi-dimensional analysis, and how to foster independent thinking skills.
item.content:encoded:
When receiving information, immediately activate your “Critical Thinking Radar”:

  1. “Sentence Integrity Check”: First, examine the structure of the sentence.

    • Actively look for the subject: Who is making this statement? If the subject is missing, ask yourself: Who is performing this action? Who is the recipient of this state?
    • Identify passive voice and generalization: Be vigilant about the overuse of passive voice (e.g., “The problem has been solved,” without specifying who solved it) and generalization (e.g., “People believe,” without specifying which people). This is often done to obscure responsibility or create the illusion of universal consensus.

  2. Ask quick questions to uncover the underlying intent and impact of the information:

    • “Why am I seeing/hearing this?” (Tracing the Information Source):
      • What channel delivered this information to me? (Advertisement, news, social media, friend recommendation, etc.)
      • Does this channel itself have a bias or vested interest?
      • Did I actively search for it, or was it passively delivered to me?
    • “Why has this gained such high traction in the contemporary information flood?” (Analyzing Propagation Dynamics):
      • Does this information cater to a specific social emotion or anxiety?
      • Does it use narrative styles or emotional language that is easily relatable?
      • Are there signs of artificial promotion (e.g., massive forwarding, bot comments)?
    • “Who benefits from this?” (Stakeholder Analysis):
      • Who will benefit from me accepting this information? (e.g., the merchant selling the product, the institution promoting the view, the group seeking political support, etc.)
      • Is this benefit a direct economic gain, or an indirect social or political influence?
      • Is there a clear conflict of interest?
    • “What is this information ignoring? / What is it hiding?” (Identifying Information Gaps):
      • Does this information only present one side of the facts?
      • Have important background information or counter-evidence been omitted?
      • Is ambiguous or misleading language being used to conceal the truth?
    • “What is the purpose of this information? What does it want me to do?” (Behavioral Guidance Analysis):
      • Does it want me to purchase a certain product or service?
      • Does it want me to adopt a certain view or stance?
      • Does it want me to take a specific action (e.g., vote, donate, share)?
    • Focusing on the significance of “Specific People”:
      • Tracing the source: Instead of passively accepting “Research shows,” ask: Which research institution? Which researcher? What is their methodology? What is their past research record? Is there a conflict of interest?
      • Evaluating expert qualifications and stance: When hearing “Experts believe,” ask: Which expert? What is their professional background and qualification in this field? Have they publicly declared their stance or vested interests?
      • Wary of anonymous “experts” and “research”: “Experts” who are unwilling to disclose their specific identity, or “research” from unknown sources, often have lower credibility.

  3. Slow down your reaction speed to avoid emotional decision-making:

    • Don’t immediately believe or share: Give yourself time to think and verify.
    • Be wary of tactics that create urgency and moral coercion, such as “Limited-Time Offer” or “If you don’t share, you’re not Chinese.”
    • Control your emotions, preventing judgment from being swayed by fear, anger, anxiety, etc.

  4. Actively seek multiple information sources for cross-verification:

    • Don’t rely on a single source.
    • Look for sources from different backgrounds and perspectives to compare.
    • Pay attention to the views of authoritative institutions and professionals, but maintain a critical eye.

  5. Cultivate the habit of questioning authority and “common sense”:

    • Dare to challenge so-called “expert opinions” and “universal knowledge.”
    • Test the truthfulness of information with evidence and logic, rather than blindly trusting authority or what is habitually accepted.

  6. The debate between Einstein and Bohr fully illustrates the following points:

    • Even in the most top-tier fields, there are different viewpoints and interpretations: Science is not monolithic; even authoritative scientists may hold different understandings and explanations when facing complex problems. Scientific progress is often achieved through this debate and questioning.
    • “Authority” does not mean absolute correctness: Both Einstein and Bohr are authorities, but their views are not entirely correct, or rather, they are exploring different facets of the truth. Their debate prompts people to think about and understand quantum mechanics more deeply.
    • Selective citation can be misleading: As you mentioned, advertisers or anyone with a specific stance can completely selectively cite the views of Einstein or Bohr to support their arguments while ignoring the other party’s voice. This creates the illusion of “authoritative support” for the audience, making them believe that a certain view is absolute truth.

  7. Common Propaganda Tricks:

    • Seeking “Favorable Experts”: They look for experts whose views align with their product or philosophy and heavily promote these experts’ “authoritative endorsement.”
    • Ignoring or Devaluing Opposition: For experts or research holding differing opinions, they selectively ignore them or use various means to diminish their credibility.
    • Creating the illusion of “Scientific Proof”: They use vague phrases like “Scientific research shows,” or “Certified by XX authoritative institution,” making consumers believe that their product or philosophy is fully supported by science, when in reality, it might just be taken out of context or citing a controversial study.

Internalizing these questions and thought patterns as habits requires continuous practice. Initially, you may need to consciously remind yourself, but over time, these steps will gradually integrate into your information processing flow, allowing you to more acutely identify and resist linguistic manipulation.

item.title: The sole source of wealth: The value of production and time
item.description: Explore the true source of wealth and the importance of time as the ultimate means of production, revealing how to achieve financial freedom through production, sales, and investment.
item.content:encoded:
The Only Normal Source of Wealth is Production

However, the core reason why the vast majority of people fail is not because they don’t engage in production, nor is it because they never accumulate. Rather, it is because they fail to accumulate for a sufficiently long time, resulting in insufficient capital, and thus they fail to acquire or master true wealth.

Life should be centered around production. Everything else, no matter what it is, must be ranked after it. Nothing is more important than production—at least, until basic necessities are met.

What Exactly Are the Means of Production?

  • Time is the only means of production owned by the proletariat. Time is incompressible, time is uncrossable, and time is always indispensable.
  • You must produce goods and services that can be sold. In other words, someone needs them, or even the entire society needs them, for someone to buy them. Otherwise, how good you feel your creation is is useless. If no one wants it, there is no exchange, and therefore, there is no money.

The Fundamental Reason for Life’s Hardship

To make money, you must produce, because the only legitimate source of wealth is production; conversely, if you don’t produce, you won’t earn money. Fundamentally, the difference in people’s income primarily stems from the distance from effective production. In other words, the closer you are to production, the more money you earn; or conversely, the farther you are from production, the less money you earn.

The Jobs People Dislike Doing

In the past, apprentices mostly focused on the production process; but for today’s workers, the most profitable approach might be to choose the sales process—that is, working in a sales department.

The key here is that sales income has no upper limit. This is unmatched by any other organized form of effective production. The more developed the society, the larger the market, and the richer the variety of goods and services, the more essential sales become to the creators. Therefore, many sales positions have a “performance commission incentive mechanism”—how much you earn depends on your performance. Other positions, such as administration, accounting, and logistics, generally have fixed salaries. So, if you want to earn more, you should prioritize choosing sales.

Absurdly Selling the Means of Production

Time is our ultimate means of production. The tragic thing is that 99% of people rely on directly selling their time to earn income. For the vast majority of people, their personal business model throughout their lives is simply selling their time without any processing. Then, they desperately compete at this level, striving to have the highest unit price for their time—that’s all.

The Business Sense Not Taught in School

Customer Lifetime Value refers to the profit you can earn from a single customer who buys your product or service throughout their entire life.

  • The shorter the time cost, the harder it is to make money.

For a restaurant, it is actually a quite good business for the average person, and the probability of success is quite high. However, from the perspective of time cost, this business is not the most profitable. It has a certain learning time cost, and while the daily production time cost is not high, it requires continuous production, and every sale incurs a certain time cost.

In comparison,

Creating a book is relatively much more profitable because, although the learning time cost is relatively high (research and preparation), there is also some production time cost (the writing process). But the sales time cost and the reproduction time cost are zero for the author.

Money is a Social Ledger

  • From the essential nature of a social ledger, it can be seen that money is actually the debt of the entire society. It represents what society owes you or the services it owes you. If you are very poor and lack money, it actually represents that you owe society a lot. You have made little contribution to society.

  • Money can factually store anything, so, of course, money can also be a form of means of production storage.

  • Money is a means of production. And, it is simultaneously a form of storage.

  • Money is the most flexible means of production.

Money Has Two Different Uses

  • For most people, money has only one use: consumption.
  • The second, and far more important, use of money is: investment.

The desire to invest grows from nothing and becomes increasingly strong. It automatically overwhelms the desire to consume, to the point where, without realizing it, you naturally use more money for investment rather than consumption, unless it is a necessary consumption.

Consumption is naturally joyful because desires are satisfied. But actually, investment is also joyful; it is also a way of satisfying desires, and perhaps it should be even more joyful.

Knowledge is like this, and useful knowledge is even more so. Once you learn it, you cannot forget it. It is difficult for you now to waste money carelessly because you feel it should be used to produce; it is difficult for you to hate the rich because you know they are creditors; it is difficult for you to ignore financial management because you know money is the storage of all things, and your freedom is stored there; it is difficult for you to be content with simply selling your time because you know that is the worst personal business model;

The Fundamental Principle of Producing with Money

The essence of investment is actually lending and receiving interest. Even the core of finance is merely interest; and the entire financial market is driven by and exists solely because of interest rates.

  • Money is actually a form of means of production.
  • Interest is the compensation for the opportunity cost of capital.

Just like time, capital is an exclusive resource. This means that its use incurs an opportunity cost.

Regarding Borrowing Money

All money lent to relatives and friends is essentially given away; do not expect them to pay it back.

People who know how to produce with money cannot just lend money out casually because their opportunity cost is relatively higher. Upon deeper reflection, many people lend money to others not because they consider themselves generous or benevolent, but because of ignorance or incompetence. The opportunity cost of the money they hold is actually zero, so they don’t care much. Of course, this statement is difficult to hear, but the logic is sound.

Equity is Essentially Equivalent to Debt

  • From the company’s perspective, the company has borrowed a sum of money that never needs to be repaid.
  • From the lender’s perspective, there are suddenly many benefits: higher returns and stronger liquidity.

The Fundamental Difference Between Investment and Speculation

In the stock market, all investors are traders, but factually, not all traders are investors. Only a tiny minority of traders follow a long-term holding strategy, while the vast majority of traders engage in frequent trading. What is the difference? Only investors consider time as a necessary component of the means of production, whereas the vast majority of traders—let’s call them “speculators”—do not have time in their means of production.

Time is the Only Path to Development.

Traders play completely different games in the same arena. Speculators participate in what I believe is the worst kind of limited game, called a “zero-sum game”: the money earned is actually the money lost by others. But investors are different; if they succeed, they earn the “result of development.” What they participate in is actually an “infinite game.”

The Mirror Effect of Investment Risk

I am too lazy to even look at financial reports because the best companies are the ones that fake their financial reports the least. I have a background in accounting, so it’s not that I can’t understand financial reports; I just feel that picking stocks by looking at financial reports is like trying to find gold in a pile of garbage. But the problem is, the gold mountain is standing right there, so why bother? The way ordinary people choose stocks is simple: first, try to choose the best goods in life. Then, not only buy the goods, but also buy the stock simultaneously.

The Actual Shape of Individual Time

Time is like a container, and inside it are all the people who have lived up to the present, and all the things they have done. Obviously, the size of each person’s time container is different.

This container of time has a starting point and an endpoint, but between the start and the end, time is more like a pipeline than just a straight line. Some people do more things in a unit of time and are more efficient; therefore, this person’s time is different from others’ time—it has a larger diameter, a thicker pipe. Some people do nothing meaningful for a long time; in that period, this person’s time is merely a straight line.

What should we do to make money? Produce, sell, invest. In any case, we absolutely cannot waste this ultimate means of production, time, on things that yield no output.

How to Do More Things

  • After spending time to earn money, we must do more things.
  • More precious than financial freedom is actually time freedom.

For those without production capacity, time is merely a ray—instantaneously having no area, long-term having no volume; time is not really a means of production. Therefore, time can only be “bored,” bored to the point of “waste,” and must reach the point of being “killed.” For those with production capacity, time is simply too beautiful; it can be used to create anything, do countless things, and even family affection or love can be “fermented” with time. Furthermore, as production efficiency increases, the possibilities of time become more numerous and greater. This is probably the most exciting reason why we are obsessed with learning and unwilling to learn any skill!

Factors Acting Against Production

If you are a producer, or even an effective producer, or even just someone aspiring to be a producer, you must know that there are things that are naturally “anti-production” and absolutely must be avoided. First are drugs and gambling. The ultimate victims of these two things are likely to start innocently, based on the naive idea of “just trying” or “just playing,” holding the侥幸 (lucky chance) mentality that “it won’t happen again.” Little do they know, these two things should not even be touched.

Of course, more common than drugs and gambling is vanity. The definition of vanity can be very clear: money used for consumption was not earned through one’s own production, yet one is not ashamed of it but is proud of it.

Wealth Index = Own Production Income / Own Consumption Expenditure

  • If a person’s Wealth Index = 1, they are neither poor nor rich;
  • If Wealth Index < 1, they are poor, and the smaller the Wealth Index, the poorer they are;
  • If Wealth Index > 1, they are wealthy, and the larger the Wealth Index, the richer they are.

Many so-called wealthy people have the actual dilemma that their consumption expenditure is very high, while their production income is equal to 0, or even less than 0.

Some people genuinely earn money through effective production, but they often fall back into poverty—as the old saying goes, “Seeing the high building, seeing the banquet, seeing the building collapse.” The core reason for falling back into poverty is always the same: the growth rate of consumption expenditure far exceeds the growth rate of production income.

In my words, never increase your consumption level too quickly.

In the more than 40 years since the Reform and Opening Up, a large number of so-called “middle classes” have appeared. But once the economy declines, the vast majority of them fall back into poverty overnight. What happened? It’s not that they didn’t earn money; their problem is that they earned money but failed to control their spending. Too many expenditures in life are not necessities but stem from desires from various angles. Desire has no end; if it is not properly controlled, it actually has the power to make anyone fall back into poverty, no matter how strong their production capacity is.

Wealth Gap is Inevitable

Every sedan requires at least 4 people to carry it; there must inevitably be poor people, and society needs poor people to function normally.

Basic Principles for Improving Efficiency

The act of learning actually includes at least four levels: learning, practicing, applying, and creating. Therefore, just learning without practicing is a waste of time and is the fundamental reason why most people fail to learn. What you learn, you must use; what you learn, you must practice. The process of practice is actually the only way to improve efficiency. Through massive iteration (not just repetition), continuous accumulation, and continuous improvement. Efficiency can never happen overnight, because efficiency must be developed.

Unexpected things will certainly happen in life, and you will encounter bad people and bad events, but these are external factors. Their existence or appearance has already damaged my development; you absolutely cannot let them further devour my ultimate means of production. After all, all my wealth, whether material or spiritual, comes from my time, or more accurately, from the volume of my time. What time do I have to waste? What reason do I have to waste it on them? At all times, focusing on improving efficiency is the main thing.

Summary

  • Wealth comes from production, and it comes from oneself;
  • Time is the ultimate means of production;
  • Money is the storage of all things;
  • Money is the most flexible means of production.

In this increasingly better era, as long as you spend your time on self-study, production, sales, and investment, you can earn money, and there are still many things worth doing.

item.title: The stock market is a powerful wealth-building tool
item.description: The stock market is a powerful wealth-building tool and you should be investing in it. But realize the market and the value of your shares will sometimes drop dramatically. This is absolutely normal and to be expected. When it happens, ignore the drops and buy more shares. This will be much, much harder than you think. People all around you will panic. The news media will be screaming Sell, Sell, Sell!

item.title: Those scarce goods must be allocated through price.
item.description: This paper explores economic phenomena across various dimensions, including investment principles, economic theories, and consumer psychology, revealing the profound impact of risk, return, supply-demand dynamics, and social behavior on economic decision-making.
item.content:encoded:
I even believe that all ports must be allocated through price. In a commodity economy, equivalent exchange is the foundation that ensures smooth transactions.

The Difference Between Working and Investing

Using money to make money, rather than using time to exchange for money, is the biggest difference between working and investing.

Average Investment Level: Pursuing Relative Victory

In the field of investment, achieving absolute victory is not easy, but relative victory is more realistic. Investors who achieve relative victory can become profitable, while those who achieve absolute victory may become masters. However, mastery is not achieved overnight, nor can everyone become a master. Therefore, for ordinary investors, becoming a relative winner should be the main goal.

The Relationship Between Rate of Return and Time Horizon

“Investment” refers to putting an individual’s money, time, or energy resources into something expected to yield a profitable or satisfactory return. The return demanded by investors depends on how much investment risk they perceive. If an investment is extremely risky, investors usually expect a higher rate of return.

Time and Liquidity: Key Factors Affecting Returns

Risk factors include Time and Liquidity. The longer the time required for an investment, the higher its rate of return should be. The longer others occupy your funds, the greater the possibility of capital loss due to unforeseen events. As an investor, you would want this risk to be compensated.

Furthermore, investors must also consider the liquidity of the funds. Liquidity refers to the ease of investing and withdrawing capital from an asset. When you urgently need money, can you quickly withdraw funds from the invested company? If yes, the investment has high liquidity, or the asset is easily convertible into cash; conversely, it has low liquidity.

Applicability of Installment Payments

Due to the existence of uncertain factors, installment payments may be a more suitable choice.

Xiao Chen is deeply in love, but his income is modest, making it difficult to meet his girlfriend Zhenzhen’s material needs. Today is his girlfriend’s 20th birthday, and he must give her a gift no matter what. He gathered a sum of money, bought a gold ring, and wrote on the card:

“Dear Zhenzhen, Happy Birthday! And I wish you happiness on all holidays from today until we get married!”

Stock Market Bottom Fishing: High-Risk Operations Require Caution

An old guy, in order to catch the boat, drove to the pier at the fastest speed. When he arrived, he found the boat had already left the shore. He locked the car door and immediately jumped onto the boat at the speed of a hundred-meter sprint, the action flowing seamlessly without any pause. His action startled everyone on the boat, and the captain said in confusion, “Sir… the boat hasn’t even docked yet…”

Bottom Fishing refers to the strategy of buying when the stock price has dropped to its lowest point, especially after a sharp decline in a short period, expecting the price to rebound quickly. Buying the cheapest stock is an opportunity all investors aspire to, and it is the profit model adhered to by value investors. However, there is no clear standard for “cheapest” or “bottom” price. Bottom fishing is often a description of buying at an already occurred low point, but it is difficult to judge what future level will be the true bottom. Furthermore, the rapid decline of some stock prices is not necessarily due to undervaluation, but rather because the company’s fundamentals genuinely have problems. If you buy at this time, the stock price may not only fail to rebound quickly but may also fall further due to unclear fundamentals.

Investment master Peter Lynch once said, “Don’t bottom fish.” This means that if an investor is confident that the company’s fundamentals have no major issues and the stock price has fallen below a reasonable valuation level, they can consider buying without trying to predict the bottom.

Moral Hazard: The Hidden Danger of Selfish Behavior

Moral Hazard is not synonymous with moral decay; rather, it refers to actions taken by individuals engaged in economic activities that are detrimental to others while maximizing their own utility. Alternatively, it can be said that when one party in a contract does not fully bear the risk consequences, they will engage in selfish behavior to maximize their own utility. This concept was proposed by Western economists in the 1980s and belongs to the field of economic philosophy.

Moral Hazard manifests in various forms, the most common of which are the following two:

  1. Deliberately Causing Insurance Accidents For example, deliberately causing cargo loss or personal injury to defraud insurance claims. This behavior is becoming increasingly prevalent in our country, especially in life insurance, where cases have occurred of insuring first and then killing the insured person to obtain the insurance payout, posing a threat to social stability.

  2. Deliberately Exaggerating the Degree of Loss When an insurance accident occurs, the insured should immediately notify the insurer and take measures to mitigate the loss. However, some people, in order to defraud more insurance money, do not try their best to mitigate the loss but deliberately exaggerate it. For example, after a ship strikes a reef, the owner bribes the captain to deliberately steer the ship toward the reef, causing severe grounding, which makes fraud easier to achieve.

Productivity Advantage in Competition

Whoever has higher productivity is the one who can win in competition. As the saying goes: “I can fight with a broom handle, the problem is, the Northern guys won’t!”

Monetary Attributes of BTC

Currency is a specific commodity that fixedly serves as a general equivalent, possessing functions such as a medium of circulation, a means of payment, and a means of store of value. It can satisfy the needs of commodity production and exchange, as well as the need to hold wealth in monetary form.

Never Drink Milk Proactively Given to You by a Miser

There is no free lunch in the world. When faced with a sudden windfall, one must remain sober and be less inclined to feel cheap in the face of huge economic benefits.

Supply and Demand are Mutually Causal

If there are no good men in the dance hall, will there be good women in the dance hall?

Say’s Law: Supply Creates Demand

Say’s Law, also known as the Market Law, states that under normal circumstances, a supply in the market will generate demand for it. Brodeur provides the explanation that any product in the supply market drives the distribution of money during its production process, such as purchasing raw materials, paying freight, and distributing wages. This distributed money will eventually reappear in the form of demand, thus forming a cycle between supply and demand.

Keynesianism: Demand Creates Supply

The British economist Keynes proposed a view completely opposite to Say’s Law in the 1930s: that demand can create its own supply. He believed that free mechanisms cannot guarantee stable economic growth and full employment, necessitating stronger government intervention. When demand is insufficient, the government should take measures to stimulate demand, thereby driving economic growth and achieving the goals of full employment and increased supply. This view is known as Keynes’ Law.

Customer Concession Value: The Difference Between Total Value and Total Cost

Customer Concession Value refers to the difference between the total customer value and the total customer cost. Total customer value includes product value, service value, personnel value, and image value; while total customer cost covers monetary, time, energy, and mental costs. One way to increase customer concession value is to increase the total value purchased by the customer.

Consumption Imitation Effect: Influence of Surroundings

Our consumption expenditure is often influenced by those around us. For example, a young man might not wear the same clothes as his grandfather, but he will wear the same clothes, carry the same shoulder bag, and style the same haircut as his classmates or colleagues. This is the consumption imitation effect.

Snob Effect: The Charm of Scarcity and Expense

The Snob Effect refers to consumers preferring goods that only a few people can enjoy or that are unique. The fewer people who own a certain snobbish good, the greater the demand for that good. Fine art, specially designed sports cars, and custom-made clothing are typical snobbish goods. The value consumers derive from them usually stems from the privilege, status, and sense of honor brought about by the fact that “almost no one owns the same thing as me.”

Poor Quality Assets: Worse Than Having Nothing

Worse than having nothing are assets that could potentially bring losses at any time. Taking a car as an example, suppose someone gives you a BMW, and the other party pays the down payment; you only need to repay the mortgage monthly. However, you face not only high repayment pressure but also extra expenses such as fuel costs, maintenance fees, and upkeep costs. If you sell the car at this time, the price has often already fallen, and the proceeds are insufficient to repay the loan.

Nowadays, real estate also has a tendency to become a poor quality asset. Negative assets mean not only having nothing but also owing a large debt to the bank. For example, if someone purchases a house with a market price of 1.5 million RMB, and the current market price has fallen to 900,000 RMB, but the mortgage loan and interest owed are as high as 1 million RMB, then the negative asset ratio is 10%.

Structural Unemployment: The Dilemma of Mismatched Supply and Demand

An older unmarried man encountered an older unmarried woman in the park and presented the upper couplet: “Having a body of ox strength, but no land to cultivate.” The woman immediately responded with the lower couplet: “Uselessly occupying three feet of good land, with no one to cultivate it.” This is a vivid depiction of structural unemployment: mismatched supply and demand leading to idle resources.

item.title: Producer Surplus and Consumer Surplus
item.description:
When discussing economics, Producer Surplus is an important concept. It refers to the difference between the actual income received by a producer or supplier when selling goods in the market at a certain price, and the minimum income they expected when willing to sell those goods at that price.

Simply put, Producer Surplus is the net gain of the producer in a transaction. Its calculation involves two key factors:

Producer’s Supply Price: This refers to the price at which the producer is willing to sell the goods or services. Typically, the producer’s supply price is related to their marginal cost (the extra cost of producing one unit of goods), because they hope to at least cover the production cost.
item.content:encoded:
When discussing economics, Producer Surplus is an important concept. It refers to the difference between the actual income received by a producer or supplier when selling goods in the market at a certain price, and the minimum income they expected when willing to sell those goods at that price.

Simply put, Producer Surplus is the net gain of the producer in a transaction. Its calculation involves two key factors:

Producer’s Supply Price: This refers to the price at which the producer is willing to sell the goods or services. Typically, the producer’s supply price is related to their marginal cost (the extra cost of producing one unit of goods), because they hope to at least cover the production cost.

Market Price: This refers to the price the buyer is willing to pay, which is the market price of the goods or services.

The calculation formula for Producer Surplus is as follows:

Producer Surplus = Producer’s Supply Price - Market Price

Producer Surplus represents the net gain obtained by the producer when selling goods at a lower supply price. Producer Surplus occurs when the market price is higher than the producer’s supply price, because the producer sells the goods at a lower price but receives a higher actual income. If the market price is lower than the producer’s supply price, the Producer Surplus will be negative, meaning the producer may incur a loss in the transaction.

Producer Surplus is very important for understanding market operation and the supply-demand relationship. In a free market, the balance of supply and demand determines the market price, and Producer Surplus helps us understand the producer’s profitability at different price levels. When the market is in equilibrium, Producer Surplus is maximized, meaning the producer achieves maximum profit.

Okay, Consumer Surplus is an economic term that refers to the economic benefit or value obtained by consumers when purchasing goods or services. Its calculation method is:

Consumer Surplus = Consumer’s Reservation Price (Expected Price) - Actual Paid Price

For a simple example, assume the reservation price for an item is 100 Yuan for the consumer. If the actual market price is 80 Yuan, then the Consumer Surplus obtained by that consumer when purchasing the item is 100 - 80 = 20 Yuan.

Consumer Surplus reflects the net gain obtained by the consumer after purchasing goods or services. The larger the Consumer Surplus, the higher the economic utility obtained by the consumer. Increasing Consumer Surplus can usually raise total social welfare. The government employs many measures to increase Consumer Surplus, such as subsidies, tax incentives, etc.

item.title: What should I do if I want to earn profit beyond the value of the labor itself?
item.description: In a free competitive market, when the wage level of a certain profession or industry is higher than the value deserved by the labor output or skills for that job, it attracts more people to study that profession and enter that market. As the supply increases, the number of workers in the market grows, which subsequently causes the wage level to decrease, eventually approaching the value deserved by the labor output.
item.content:encoded:
In a free competitive market, when the wage level of a certain profession or industry is higher than the value deserved by the labor output or skills for that job, it attracts more people to study that profession and enter that market. As the supply increases, the number of workers in the market grows, which subsequently causes the wage level to decrease, eventually approaching the value deserved by the labor output.

This phenomenon is known in economics as the “Marginal Productivity Theory.” It posits that there is a relationship between the wage level and the marginal output of labor (which is the increase in output generated by adding one unit of labor). When a certain profession’s wage is higher than its marginal output, it attracts more people to join, thereby increasing the labor supply, which in turn lowers the wage level until the marginal output and the wage level reach equilibrium.

This phenomenon is common across many professions and industries. When supply and demand in the market tend towards equilibrium, the wage level usually tends towards the value of the marginal output—this is the situation you mentioned where profit approaches zero. In the long run, the market forms a relatively stable equilibrium state, and the wage level adjusts to match the skills, labor output, and market demand.

This also explains why continuous learning and skill improvement are extremely important for individuals to achieve success and obtain better compensation in the workplace. By constantly improving one’s skills and knowledge, an individual can maintain competitiveness in a fierce market and achieve better economic returns.

If you wish to earn extra profit beyond the value of the labor itself in the labor market, you can consider the following strategies:

Differentiation and Specialization: Find the field or specific skill you excel in, and continuously refine it to become an expert. Through differentiation and specialization, you can provide higher quality and more specialized services, thereby creating higher market value for yourself.

Creating Unique Value: Identify the pain points or needs in the market and provide unique solutions. Understand the customer’s true needs and offer services that exceed their expectations. This can win you more customers and positive word-of-mouth, leading to extra profit beyond the value of the labor itself.

Building a Personal Brand: Establish your visibility and authority in the industry through effective branding and personal promotion. A reputable and credible personal brand can bring you more business opportunities and chances, potentially leading to higher returns.

Mastering Composite Skills: Learning and mastering skills across multiple fields allows you to become a versatile individual. Possessing multiple skills increases your flexibility and adaptability, better meeting market demands, which brings you more opportunities and potential profits.

Innovation and Leadership: Continuously innovating and leading teams to achieve goals can bring you more business opportunities and project collaborations, thereby creating extra profit for you.

It is important to emphasize that pursuing extra profit beyond the value of the labor itself is not easy; it requires a significant investment of time, effort, and resources. Furthermore, success is not achieved overnight; it requires continuous effort and ongoing learning and growth. The key is to find the development path and strategy that suits you and continuously optimize and adjust it through practice. In a fiercely competitive market, only by continuously enhancing your value can you gain more opportunities and profits in the workplace.

item.title: Never use short-term solutions to deal with long-term problems.
item.description: I absolutely cannot let people think I am stingy. So, I frequently invite friends to restaurants; I also need a luxury car to display my status; furthermore, I must pay some other expenses—taxes. Finally, I have to turn to this great invention: the credit card. With a credit card, I don’t have to pay myself; the people at the credit card company will help me pay, at least temporarily… After that, I heard someone say, “He is truly a winner in life; he is living a first-class life.” I was living a first-class life: not drinking sparkling wine—only champagne; not eating a steak—only prime tenderloin. I wanted to live like a rich person in a futuristic world. And soon, the past began to constantly bother me in the form of bills, collection letters, and high loan interest rates. As a high-performing, high-income salesperson, I was always able to get a new credit card. So, I started making revolving payments, meaning I would get a new credit card and then use the new card to pay off the bill of the old credit card. Just like that, I spiraled into a downward financial state.

item.description: Achieving financial security requires that the most important standard—the availability of money—is met. You must have a daily income. Therefore, it is best to put your money in a safe or invest it in a cash fund. You should not take risks until you achieve financial security. Consequently, you should choose low-risk investment projects. However, even so, you must pay attention to managing potential risks. Never put all your money into a single investment project, even if “all your funds” only total 1,000 Euros. Remember, managing risk means increasing the opportunity for profit. The 40:40:20 Principle Guarantees Financial Security To achieve financial security, you must change the allocation ratio of your money. Although most of the money must still be put into low-risk investments, you can allocate 40% to moderately risky investments. If you consistently hold this money without using it, the risk will be greatly reduced through the effect of “average cost return.” The remaining 20% can be invested in high-risk projects, which involves speculative funds such as emerging market funds or national funds, as well as all special funds and corporate participation funds. The risk of these funds can also be reduced over time through the effect of “average cost return.” On the other hand, your probability of profit is also extremely high. One important point is: you absolutely cannot put the money used to guarantee your financial security into high-risk or speculative projects. You must not touch this money. The investments you make must guarantee that your financial security is never affected.

item.title: Little Dog Money Summary
item.description: Some people who read this book cannot take in what you say, so there is no change. Others, after reading it, begin to be smart about geography and finance, and they will have a happier and richer life.
item.content:encoded:
The Foundation of Wealth Building

Financial freedom is a goal that anyone today can achieve, of course, this requires us to have the courage to pursue the life we truly desire. As a famous saying goes: “It is not the difficulty that makes us give up, but rather that we give up, which makes it seem so difficult.”

If we keep the laws of money in mind, we will find that our financial situation is steadily improving. Nothing can stop a mindset that aligns with the times. This also applies to everyone’s life. Nothing can stop us from enjoying the right we are born with—wealth. A life of dignity and financial comfort aligns with our natural laws. As long as we don’t give up, nothing can prevent us from reaching this goal.

Making a Dream Album

To achieve financial freedom, we must have motivation. Therefore, the first thing we must do is think up 10 reasons (wishes) why we want to become wealthy, and write them down. This will be the driving force for our actions.

Next, from these 10 reasons for wanting to become wealthy, select the top 3 most important ones. Don’t set yourself too many goals, as that might be unrealistic. Human desires are endless, and we need to distinguish between primary and secondary, determining which are the most important goals. After setting the goals, we must find ways to achieve them.

One method taught by Qianqian to Jia is to use a Dream Album and a Dream Piggy Bank: the Dream Album is used to collect photos related to your wishes, and you paste them into the album.

Looking at the Album Daily

The act of thinking through pictures and imagining the scenarios where you achieve your wishes is called “visualization.”

Preparing a Dream Piggy Bank

Prepare a piggy bank for each dream, and write your dream on it. Once the piggy bank is ready, save every penny you save into it.

When Jia doubted whether the Dream Album would be effective, Qianqian said: “Curiosity is good, but it must never hinder your actions. Too many people hesitate in their actions simply because they feel they haven’t fully understood the matter. Putting it into practice is much more useful than pure thinking.”

When we question whether this fantasy is a “pipe dream,” we need to know that “successful people are successful because they always dream of the day they succeed, constantly imagining the situation when they have achieved their dreams. Of course, people cannot remain stuck in dreams.”

“Learning is the process of recognizing new concepts and new ideas. If people always consider problems using the same way of thinking, they will always get the same results. Don’t jump to conclusions before you have done it.”

People without imagination find it difficult to achieve great things. The more effort we put into something, the greater the possibility of success. But most people put their energy into things they don’t like, instead of imagining what they hope to gain.

Don’t approach it with a “let’s try” mindset; take concrete action! If you only approach it with a “let’s try” mindset, it will only end in failure, and we will achieve nothing. ‘Trying’ is merely an excuse; before we even try, we have already prepared an escape route for ourselves. There is no option to ’try’; there are only two choices—to do it or not to do it."

Success Journal

When we do something, we need sufficient self-confidence. Our level of confidence determines whether we believe in our ability and whether we believe in ourselves. If we fundamentally don’t believe we can do it, we won’t even start, and if we don’t start, we will gain nothing."

Therefore, we need to keep a “Success Journal.” The “Success Journal” is similar to a diary; record all the things you have successfully done in it, writing down at least 5 personal achievements every day, no matter how small. The main purpose of doing this is to help us boost our self-confidence.

At the beginning, we might feel it’s difficult, and we might ask ourselves, “Can this or that thing really be counted as an achievement?” In this case, our answer should be affirmative. Being overly confident is much better than being insufficiently confident."

When we encounter problems:

a. Still stick to your idea Everyone can do this when things are normal. It is only when true difficulties arise that the difference becomes clear. Only a few people can firmly implement their plans. Very successful people even have the ability to perform exceptionally when things are at their most difficult.

b. When progress is smooth Even when everything is progressing very smoothly, you must firmly stick to your plan.

c. The 72-Hour Rule When we decide to do something, we must complete it within 72 hours, otherwise, we are likely to never do it again."

“How much money a person earns is linked to their self-confidence. Furthermore, whether their experiences are focused within their scope of ability or placed outside of what they can achieve is also very important. Without a Success Journal, we won’t think about in which areas we are suited to earn money.”

Often, our inability to act stems from the psychology of fear. Fear always appears when we imagine how things might go wrong. The more we think about the possibility of failure, the more afraid we become. But when we look at our Success Journal, we notice the successful things, and naturally, we think about how to do them."

Earning and Saving Money

When Qianqian encouraged Jia to bravely earn money, she told the story of a young boy named Darryl. Darryl became a millionaire at the age of 17 through personal effort, making him a role model for Jia.

In Darryl’s story, a businessman gave Darryl (Jia’s role model) advice on earning money:

  1. Figure out what you like, and then figure out how to earn money from it.
  2. Solve a problem for others, and you will earn a lot of money;
  3. Focus your energy on what you know, what you can do, and what you possess.
  4. Before buying something, ask yourself, “Is this really necessary?”

Mr. Jin, when guiding Jia not to spend all the money she had immediately, told the story of a goose that lays golden eggs:

A goose raised by a farmer lays a golden egg every day. The farmer was very greedy and hoped the goose would lay at least two golden eggs every day. In a fit of pique, he killed the goose, and from then on, he never received another golden egg. The goose is the principal, and the golden egg is the interest. The farmer’s biggest mistake was not “killing” his “goose.”

Expenditure and income are directly proportional; the higher the income, the higher the expenditure, unless you learn to allocate your assets reasonably and learn to spend within your means.

Advice for Those in Debt:

a. Destroy all credit cards Spending with a credit card costs more than spending with cash.

b. Pay the minimum installment amount within the allowed limit The higher the installment amount, the less living money you have left each month. Often, people underestimate how high their living expenses are, and they might take out new loans to pay off old ones when a large expense occurs.

c. For consumer loans For loans for goods in daily life, such as a TV loan, it is best not to apply for it first. If you do apply, save half of the money remaining after deducting living expenses, and use the other half to pay the consumer loan.

Fund Allocation

The author suggests that we can divide our income into Daily Expenses (10%) + Dream Goals (40%) + Golden Goose Account (50%). This means we can save 50% of our income, and this money should not be easily touched; it is like the goose mentioned earlier that lays golden eggs, allowing money to generate more money.

Of the remaining 50%, besides the 10% needed for daily life, the remaining 40% is saved to achieve the dreams we want, such as buying a phone as a reward for yourself, or going on a trip, etc. This amount is up to you to manage and plan; remember to allocate it reasonably.

Golden Goose: From the story of laying golden eggs, the “goose” refers to the money (savings value), and the “golden egg” refers to the interest.

Never kill your goose, and don’t use all your money to pay off loans, leaving yourself with nothing. Having nothing is not our goal; our goal is to achieve the initial 3 wishes or accumulate the savings.

Passive Income

Investment Tips:

  1. Invest money in a safe place.
  2. Money should lay many “golden eggs” (choose high interest, with the highest dividends coming from stocks).
  3. Investment should be simple and clear, easy to operate.

The 72 Rule:

Divide 72 by the annual profit percentage of the investment, and the resulting number is the number of years required for that money to double.

Divide 72 by a certain inflation rate, and you can find out how many years it will take for the money to lose half its value.

When the market declines, losses only occur when you actually sell the fund.

A fund has an indicator—the Fluctuation Rate (Volatility): a lower fluctuation rate means higher safety and more stable profit growth. Funds generally last 5 to 10 years; the market always has ups and downs, but the overall trend is upward, so you can check the market after 5 or 10 years.

72 / Return Rate = Time to Double 72 / Inflation Rate = Time to Half Value 115 Rule: 115 / Return Rate = Time to Double

Controlling Risk

Cash Reserves are Necessary

You cannot put all your money into stocks or funds; you must reserve some cash to have liquid funds, so that when the stock market declines, you can buy appropriately at the right time. The remaining reserve cash can be invested in short-term income projects, such as daily deposits. Bank passbooks are merely money-swallowing machines; their returns are often less than the losses caused by inflation. Some savings accounts have high interest rates, but they require keeping the cash in the bank for a relatively long time, so the author does not recommend relying solely on bank passbooks.

Qianqian’s Words

Some people who read this book do not absorb what you say, and thus make no changes. Others, after reading it, begin to manage their finances wisely, and they will lead happier and wealthier lives.

item.title: When in debt, you also need a goose.
item.description:
First, people who are in debt should destroy all their credit cards. This is because most people spend much more when using credit cards than when using cash.

The second piece of advice is that one should repay each loan installment as little as possible. In most cases, they haven’t estimated that living expenses will be so high. When they must purchase a new car or something in the house breaks down, they have to pay for these things by taking out another loan.

  2. If you only approach it with a “let’s try it” mindset, you will ultimately end in failure and achieve nothing.
  3. “Trying” is an excuse. Before you even do it, you have already prepared an escape route for yourself.
  4. If you cannot test it, you only have two choices: do it or don’t do it.
  5. The most critical factor in whether you can earn money is not whether you have a good idea.
  6. How smart you are is not the main reason; the determining factor is your level of confidence.
  7. You must first clarify where your interests lie, and then consider how to earn money through them.
  8. You must do things every day without interruption that are highly significant to your future.
  9. The time you spend on this will not exceed 10 minutes, but those 10 minutes will make everything different.
  10. People who are in debt should cancel all their credit cards.

  12. You should save half of the money that isn’t used for living, and use the other half to pay off debt.

  15. Poverty makes people even less fortunate.
  16. If I don’t have my “goose,” I always have to work just to earn money.
  17. But once I have a “goose,” my “money will automatically work for me.”
  18. Luck is actually just the result of sufficient preparation combined with hard work.
  19. Money only stays with those who put in the effort for it.
  20. People who acquire unjust wealth through illegal means often feel worse than when they have no money at all.
  21. Fear always appears when we imagine how things might go wrong.
  22. The more we think about the possibility of failure, the more afraid we become.
  23. But when you think toward positive goals, you will not feel fear.
  24. Whenever winter passes, spring comes, followed by summer; after every summer comes autumn, and then winter again—year after year.
  25. Just like the changes in nature, the stock exchange always experiences the changing of seasons, cycling back and forth.
  26. If you don’t do this thing today, you will never know what you are capable of writing after putting some pressure on yourself.
  27. The things a person feels the most proud of are the ones that were the most difficult to achieve.

item.title: But Monica's parents' financial situation is getting better, isn't it?
item.description: Soon, I turned 12. Everything was still the same; we still didn’t go on vacation by the sea. Mom and Dad kept saying that business was affected by the “economic recession.” What they meant was that the domestic economic situation was the root cause of their financial problems. But I had a question: why was my friend Monica’s parents’ financial situation getting better and better, even with the same economic situation?

item.title: It's not trying, but taking action!
item.description: If you only approach things with a “try-it-out” mindset, then you will ultimately end in failure, and you will achieve nothing. Trying is purely an excuse; before you even do it, you have already prepared an escape route for yourself. If you can’t test, you only have two choices—do it or don’t do it. Too many people hesitate when doing things simply because they feel they haven’t fully grasped something. And actually putting it into practice is much smarter than pure thinking.
